subject: Coffee & Tea
title: The Invention of the Drum Roaster
description: A tiny lesson with a big payoff: The Invention of the Drum Roaster.

hook.text: The first commercial drum roaster was patented in 1849 by James Carter in Boston. It mechanized an ancient craft.

buildup.text: A rotating metal cylinder over a gas flame tumbled beans evenly. For the first time, large batches could roast uniformly.

discovery.text: Drum roasting made commercial coffee possible. Before it, each household or shop roasted its own small batches.

twist.text: German company Probat, founded in 1868, became the dominant manufacturer. Many vintage Probats still run today.

climax.text: The drum roaster turned coffee from a cottage craft into a global industry. It's still the most common roasting technology.

punchline.text: A spinning drum, even heat, massive scale. One machine built an industry.

quiz.question: Who patented the first commercial drum coffee roaster?

details.summary: The drum roaster was invented in the 19th century and revolutionized coffee production by allowing large, consistent batches. A rotating cylinder tumbles beans over a heat source, combining conduction and convection. It became the industry standard and remains so today.
details.whyItMatters: The drum roaster made consistent, high-volume coffee roasting possible for the first time. Without it, the modern coffee industry as we know it could not exist.
takeaways: Drum roasters emerged in the 1800s for commercial coffee production
A heated cylinder tumbles beans for consistent heat distribution
They remain the dominant roaster type in the coffee industry

faq.question: Who is credited with inventing the first commercial drum roaster?
faq.answer: Several inventors contributed, but Jabez Burns patented a self-emptying commercial drum roaster in 1864 in New York. His design allowed continuous operation and became the template for modern commercial roasters.

faq.question: How has the basic drum roaster design changed since the 1800s?
faq.answer: Modern drum roasters add digital temperature probes, variable-speed drives, automated airflow dampers, and data logging software. The core principle of tumbling beans in a heated drum, however, remains essentially unchanged.
